title: Truman Fires MacArthur
text:
In 1950 and 1951 General Douglas MacArthur commanded United Nations forces in Korea. After Chinese armies entered the war, President Harry Truman decided to seek a limited war and eventually a negotiated settlement, not an expansion into China. MacArthur disagreed and said so in public, repeatedly, in statements and letters that contradicted the administration's policy.

In March 1951 he issued his own ultimatum to the Chinese commanders, undercutting a peace initiative Truman was preparing. In early April a Republican congressman, Joseph Martin, read aloud in the House a letter from MacArthur criticizing the policy and ending with the phrase that there was no substitute for victory.

On April 11, 1951, Truman relieved MacArthur of command, with the backing of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The decision was hugely unpopular. MacArthur returned to ticker-tape parades and addressed Congress, and Truman's approval rating fell to historic lows.

In the Senate hearings that followed, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, Omar Bradley, defended the decision, arguing that MacArthur's strategy would mean the wrong war, at the wrong place, at the wrong time, with the wrong enemy. Civilian control over the military held.
lesson: Some decisions protect principles that matter more than your popularity. Make them clearly and accept the cost.
people: Harry S. Truman, Douglas MacArthur, Omar Bradley
source: Truman's statement of April 11, 1951; Truman, Memoirs, Volume 2; Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations Committee hearings (1951)
